What is Kafka? Core terms?

A distributed event streaming platform. Topic: a named stream of events. Partition: an ordered, append-only log and the unit of parallelism. Offset: a record's position in a partition. Broker: a server. Producer/Consumer. Consumer group: a set of consumers sharing the work. Replication factor: number of copies of each partition. Leader/follower, ISR (in-sync replicas). Cluster metadata is managed by KRaft; ZooKeeper is gone as of Kafka 4.0.
Kafka vs RabbitMQ?

Kafka | RabbitMQ
A log: messages are retained (by time or size) and can be replayed | A queue: messages are removed once acknowledged
Very high throughput, streaming, event sourcing | Complex routing (exchanges), per-message priority, RPC
Consumers pull and track their own offsets | The broker pushes to consumers
Ordered per partition | Ordered per queue
How does Kafka guarantee ordering?

Only within a partition. Send related events with the same key (e.g. orderId) so they land in the same partition. To keep that order under retries, enable idempotence (enable.idempotence=true, which permits max.in.flight ≤ 5).
Delivery semantics: at-most-once, at-least-once, exactly-once?

- At-most-once: commit the offset before processing. Messages can be lost.
- At-least-once (most common): process, then commit. Messages can be duplicated, so make consumers idempotent (a dedupe table or upserts).
- Exactly-once: idempotent producer + transactions (transactional.id) + isolation.level=read_committed. Only end-to-end within Kafka (consume-transform-produce).
What does acks=0/1/all mean?

acks=0: don't wait at all (fastest, can lose data). acks=1: wait for the leader only (lost if the leader dies before replicating). acks=all: wait for all ISRs, combined with min.insync.replicas=2 (the most durable; the default since Kafka 3.0).
What is consumer rebalancing?

When consumers join or leave or partitions change, the group coordinator reassigns partitions. During an eager rebalance consumption pauses. Cooperative (incremental) rebalancing, static membership (group.instance.id), and keeping max.poll.interval.ms larger than your processing time all reduce the disruption. Partitions can't be shared within a group, so consumers beyond the partition count sit idle.
What is consumer lag? How to handle slow consumers?

Lag is the latest offset minus the committed offset. Monitor it with Burrow, Prometheus or kafka-consumer-groups.sh --describe. Fixes: add partitions and consumers, increase concurrency, batch processing, tune max.poll.records, do heavy work asynchronously.
How do you handle failed messages (poison pills)?

Use Spring Kafka's DefaultErrorHandler with a FixedBackOff or ExponentialBackOff and send failures to a Dead Letter Topic through DeadLetterPublishingRecoverer, or use @RetryableTopic for non-blocking retry topics. Use ErrorHandlingDeserializer for bad payloads.
Retention and log compaction?

retention.ms / retention.bytes delete old segments. cleanup.policy=compact keeps only the latest value per key, which suits changelogs and state such as a user's latest profile. A null value (tombstone) deletes the key.
How many partitions should a topic have?

Base it on the target throughput divided by per-consumer throughput, plus room to grow. More partitions mean more parallelism, but also more file handles and longer leader elections. You can increase partitions but never decrease them, and increasing them changes where keys map.
What are Kafka Streams and Kafka Connect?

Kafka Streams: a Java library for stateful stream processing (map, filter, join, windowed aggregations, KTable). Kafka Connect: a framework for moving data in and out (source and sink connectors: JDBC, Debezium CDC, Elasticsearch, S3) without writing code. Schema Registry: Avro or Protobuf schemas with compatibility rules.
A topic has 3 partitions. A group has 4 consumers. What happens? What about 2 consumers?

With 4 consumers, three get one partition each, and the fourth is idle (a hot standby). With 2, one gets two partitions and the other one. Within a group, one partition goes to one consumer in the classic protocol. A second group with any size receives all messages independently.
RangeAssignor with 2 topics of 3 partitions each and 2 consumers. How many partitions does each get?

Range works per topic. For each topic, C1 gets 2 and C2 gets 1, as sorted order favours C1 both times. So C1 has 4, and C2 has 2. With many topics this skew grows. Round-robin or sticky gives 3 and 3. Range remains useful when you need partition N of two topics on one consumer, for joins.
RF=3, min.insync.replicas=2, acks=all. Two brokers die. What about reads and writes?

Partitions that have a live replica which was in the ISR stay readable through the survivor, which becomes leader if needed. Producers get NotEnoughReplicasException, as the ISR is 1 and fewer than 2. That is deliberate: it prefers refusing writes to accepting ones with only one copy. If the survivor was not in the ISR, the partition is offline unless unclean election is on.
A new consumer group joins an existing topic with default settings, and reads nothing. Why?

auto.offset.reset defaults to latest, so with no committed offset, it starts at the end and sees new messages only. Set earliest to read history. This setting applies only when there is no valid committed offset. Changing it on a running group does nothing. Also note the trap: if offsets expire or a retention delete passes the committed offset, a reset occurs, either skipping data (latest) or reprocessing (earliest).
What happens with auto-commit if the consumer crashes?

Auto-commit runs inside poll(), committing the offsets returned by the previous poll, on an interval. So in a simple synchronous loop it is at-least-once: a crash reprocesses the records since the last commit. But if you hand records to another thread, a commit may run before they finish, and a crash loses them. That is why async processing needs manual commits.
Consumers keep rebalancing, and the same messages are processed repeatedly. Why?

Classic cause: processing a batch takes longer than max.poll.interval.ms. The consumer is kicked out, its commit fails with CommitFailedException, its partitions are reassigned, and the new owner starts again from the last commit, repeating the cycle. Fix: reduce max.poll.records, raise the interval, speed up the handler, or commit per record. Other causes: GC pauses over the session timeout, frequent pod restarts (use static membership), or a retry loop inside the listener.
session.timeout.ms vs max.poll.interval.ms vs heartbeat.interval.ms?

Heartbeats run on a background thread, and tell the coordinator the process is alive; if none arrive within session.timeout.ms the member is removed. max.poll.interval.ms measures gaps between poll() calls, and detects a live process whose processing is stuck. The separation lets a slow handler run for minutes without failing liveness, while crashes are detected in seconds.
Does max.in.flight=5 risk reordering?

With idempotence off and retries on, yes: batch 1 fails, batch 2 succeeds, and batch 1's retry lands after it. The old fix was max.in.flight=1, at a throughput cost. With idempotence on, sequence numbers let the broker reject out-of-order batches, so the client retries in order, and order holds for up to 5 in flight. Setting a value above 5 with idempotence enabled is a config error.
Is send() synchronous? How do you know a record was written?

It is asynchronous: it serialises, buffers, and returns a future. It may still block, up to max.block.ms, for metadata or buffer space, which can stall a web thread when the cluster is down. Check the result through whenComplete or .get(timeout). A fire-and-forget kafka.send() in Spring silently drops failures. Calling .get() per message kills batching, so call flush() or collect futures instead.
What is the relationship between linger.ms, batch.size and delivery.timeout.ms?

A batch is sent when it reaches batch.size or has waited linger.ms, whichever comes first. It is also sent sooner if buffer memory is under pressure. delivery.timeout.ms covers the entire time from send() to final result: lingering, queuing, retries, and in-flight time. It must be at least linger.ms + request.timeout.ms. After it passes, the callback receives a timeout, and the outcome is unknown: the record may have been written.
How does adding partitions affect a running system?

It triggers a rebalance. New keys may hash to different partitions, so per-key order breaks across the change: old events for key K are in partition 2, and new ones in partition 7, read concurrently. Compacted topics and Streams state also rely on stable partitioning. If order matters, drain and move to a new topic, or over-provision at the start. Partitions cannot be reduced. To reduce, create a new topic and migrate.
How would you preserve ordering with parallel processing in one consumer?

Spring concurrency keeps order per partition, since each partition has one thread. If you need more parallelism than partitions, hash each record's key to one of N single-threaded workers, so one key always maps to one worker. Commit only offsets for which all earlier records are finished, tracking them per partition, and pause fetching when queues fill. Confluent's Parallel Consumer library implements this.
What does a poison pill do without ErrorHandlingDeserializer?

The failure occurs inside poll() before the listener sees the record. The container cannot move past it, so the consumer fails repeatedly on the same offset, flooding logs, while the partition stops. ErrorHandlingDeserializer catches the failure and passes the error to the handler, which can route the raw bytes to a DLT. The DLT publisher needs a byte array serializer to send the original unchanged.
DefaultErrorHandler vs @RetryableTopic: when do you pick each?

Use the blocking handler when order per key matters, or when retries are short. A long outage holds the partition, which is sometimes what you want: a failing dependency will fail all messages anyway. Use @RetryableTopic when records are independent and one bad record should not hold up the rest. It requires extra topics, and is at odds with batch listeners and transactions. A retry-topic consumer must wait until a record's delay has passed, and does so by pausing its partitions.
Does Kafka exactly-once include my database write?

No. Transactions cover Kafka partitions and offset commits only. In a listener that writes to a database and then commits, a crash between them repeats the record. Choices: an idempotent write keyed on a business id or (topic, partition, offset); storing the offset in the same DB transaction and seeking on start; or the outbox on the producing side. In Spring, a transaction-synchronised listener can commit the DB first, then Kafka, which narrows but does not remove the window, so dedupe is still required.
What is a zombie producer, and how is it fenced?

An instance that paused (long GC, partition) and was replaced, then resumes and writes. Both believe they are active, so an exactly-once pipeline would duplicate work. With a stable transactional.id, each initTransactions() increases the epoch. The broker rejects lower epochs with ProducerFencedException. For consumers, the generation in offset commits gives similar protection. In Spring, transaction-id-prefix builds ids per producer.
Consumer lag keeps growing. Walk through it.

- Is it all partitions or just one? One suggests a hot key or a poison record.
- Is producer rate up, or consumer rate down? Compare records-consumed-rate with incoming rate.
- Are there rebalances? Stop-the-world cycles look like lag.
- Is downstream (DB, API) slow? Time the handler. Most lag is a slow dependency.
- Fix: batch writes, scale consumers up to the partition count, and add partitions only if already at that limit.
- Recovery: temporarily add consumers. If the data is stale and disposable, skip forward with an offset reset.
Lag is measured as 0, but the data is old. How can that be?

Offset lag compares offsets, not time. A producer may be delayed: outbox stuck, CDC stopped, or stuck in linger or buffers. Under read_committed, an open transaction holds the LSO, so a consumer reads nothing new. Measure end-to-end latency by comparing a record's timestamp with processing time, not just offset lag.
Offsets in a compacted or transactional topic: why can't you assume offset + 1 is the next record?

Compaction leaves gaps, as removed records keep their offset numbers unused. Transactional topics hold control markers that occupy offsets and are never delivered. So do not compute lag as a record count and do not require contiguous offsets. Always commit lastProcessed.offset() + 1 as the next position, and let the consumer jump gaps.
Can Kafka lose acknowledged messages?

With RF 3, min ISR 2, acks=all, and unclean election off, loss needs all ISR copies to fail before the data is on disk. Since Kafka does not fsync each message, a simultaneous power loss of all ISR nodes could lose recent data, which is why replicas belong in different racks or zones. Risky setups lose data more easily: acks=1, min ISR 1 (the default), and unclean election. Loss is also caused by retention deleting unread data, or by ignored send failures.
What is the maximum message size, and how should you handle large payloads?

The default is about 1 MB. Changing it means raising producer max.request.size, broker or topic message.max.bytes, replica.fetch.max.bytes, and consumer fetch limits. Large messages hurt memory and throughput. The usual pattern is the claim check: put the file in object storage, and publish a reference. Compression helps with repetitive payloads.
How do you delete a single user's data from Kafka for GDPR?

You cannot edit a log. On a compacted topic keyed by user, write a tombstone. On a retained topic, keep retention short enough to satisfy the deadline, or use crypto-shredding: encrypt sensitive fields with a per-user key held elsewhere, and delete the key to make the data unreadable. Best of all, keep personal data out of events and send a reference.
How do you implement delayed messages in Kafka?

Kafka has no native per-message delay. Common approaches: tiered delay topics (delay-1m, delay-1h), where a consumer pauses until each record is due; a database scheduler that publishes when the time arrives; or Spring's retry topics for retries. If delays are core to the workload, a broker with delay support or a scheduler service may be a better fit.
How do you replicate across data centres?

MirrorMaker 2, built on Connect, copies topics, configs and consumer offsets between clusters, with topic names prefixed by the source. It is asynchronous, so failover may lose recent records, and offsets differ between clusters, requiring offset translation. For zero data loss across nearby zones, use a stretch cluster with synchronous replication, at a latency cost. Active-active needs loop prevention and conflict handling.
What is the difference between a Kafka Streams KStream, KTable and GlobalKTable?

A KStream treats every record as an independent event: two records for a key both count. A KTable treats a later record as an update to the key, partitioned across instances. A GlobalKTable holds the full table on each instance, which allows lookups by a non-partition key without repartitioning, and suits small reference data. Stream-table join enriches each event with the current table value.
Kafka Streams vs Flink vs a plain @KafkaListener?

Use a plain listener for per-record work and side effects. Use Kafka Streams for joins, windows and aggregations in a Java service, with Kafka as both source and sink. Use Flink when jobs need their own cluster, complex event time handling, multiple sources, or very large state. Streams needs no new infrastructure, but its state must be restored when tasks move, so use num.standby.replicas to shorten that.
BACKWARD compatibility: can you add a required field? Which side deploys first?

No: a new reader needs a value for old records, so a new field must have a default. Deleting a field is allowed. Consumers upgrade first, since they can then read both old and new data. Registry rejects incompatible schemas when a producer tries to register them, ideally checked in CI using the Maven plugin rather than at runtime.
Why was enable.auto.commit=false not enough to make my consumer safe?

That only moves commits to Spring. With AckMode BATCH, a poll's records commit together after all succeed. With an error handler that recovers (skips) a record after retries, its offset is committed, so anything other than a DLT means loss. Calling ack.acknowledge() in a finally block, or catching all exceptions in the listener, silently acknowledges failures. Handing work to an executor and returning acknowledges work that is not done. Safety comes from commit after a durable result.
Why is Kafka fast if it writes everything to disk?

Writes land in the page cache and are appended sequentially, so "writing to disk" does not mean a synchronous seek per message. Reads of recent data are served from memory. Batching lowers per-message overhead, compression reduces bytes, and zero-copy avoids copying between kernel and user space. The broker keeps no per-consumer per-message state. See the performance section above for detail.
How would you design an order event pipeline for 100,000 events per second?

- Topic design: orders.v1, keyed by order id, 48 or more partitions, RF 3, min ISR 2, with Avro and registry.
- Producers: outbox or CDC for correctness, lz4 or zstd, linger.ms 10 to 50.
- Consumers: separate groups by purpose (billing, search, analytics), idempotent, batch writes.
- Failures: retry, DLT, replay tool, alerts on lag and DLT rate.
- Evolution: compatibility set to BACKWARD or FULL, contract checks in CI.
- Capacity: compute disk, network and partitions as in the sizing section, then load test.
- Downstream: tiered storage or a sink to S3 for long-term analytics.
When should you NOT use Kafka?

When volume is small and a database table or RabbitMQ would do, because Kafka adds real operational cost. For low-latency request/reply, per-message priority or delay, or complex broker-side routing. For queries: it is not a database, and keyed lookups need a store built from the stream. For many small topics or very large payloads, too.
Spring for Apache Kafka or Spring Cloud Stream?

Spring for Apache Kafka (KafkaTemplate, @KafkaListener) exposes Kafka directly: partitions, offsets, transactions, error handlers, seeking. Spring Cloud Stream is a higher-level binder abstraction: you write Supplier/Function/Consumer beans and bind them to destinations in configuration, and the same code can run on Kafka or RabbitMQ. It is quick for simple pipelines but hides Kafka-specific behaviour and adds another layer of configuration to debug. Most teams that are committed to Kafka use Spring Kafka directly.
Can you do request-reply over Kafka?

Yes, with ReplyingKafkaTemplate: it sends a record with REPLY_TOPIC and CORRELATION_ID headers and returns a future that completes when a reply with that correlation id arrives; the server side is a @KafkaListener with @SendTo. Each requesting instance needs its own reply partition or topic (or must filter by correlation id), and you must set timeouts. It is usually a smell: if the caller waits synchronously, HTTP or gRPC is simpler. Use it when the work must go through Kafka anyway, for example for buffering or audit.
How do you connect a Spring Boot app to a secured Kafka cluster?

Set the security protocol and SASL mechanism, with credentials from a secret store, not the repository:
spring.kafka.bootstrap-servers=broker1:9093,broker2:9093
spring.kafka.security.protocol=SASL_SSL
spring.kafka.properties.sasl.mechanism=SCRAM-SHA-512
spring.kafka.properties.sasl.jaas.config=org.apache.kafka.common.security.scram.ScramLoginModule required username="${KAFKA_USER}" password="${KAFKA_PASSWORD}";
spring.kafka.ssl.trust-store-location=file:/etc/kafka/truststore.p12
Managed services often use OAUTHBEARER or IAM-based mechanisms instead. The principal also needs ACLs: WRITE on topics it produces to, READ on topics and its consumer group, and IDEMPOTENT_WRITE/transactional id permissions where used.
What do you put in record headers vs the payload?

The payload holds the business event. Headers hold metadata needed to route or process it without deserializing: event type and schema version, a unique event id for deduplication, correlation and trace ids (traceparent), source service, and tenant id. Spring Kafka uses headers for type information (__TypeId__), retry and DLT metadata (original topic, exception message). Do not put secrets or large data in headers, and treat them as part of the contract.
How do you document and standardize events so other teams can consume them?

Schemas (Avro, Protobuf or JSON Schema) in a Schema Registry define the payload and enforce compatibility. AsyncAPI is the event equivalent of OpenAPI: it describes channels (topics), messages, keys and headers, and can generate docs and code. CloudEvents is a CNCF spec for common event metadata (id, source, type, time, subject), with a Kafka binding that maps them to headers. Also document ownership, the partition key, ordering guarantees and retention for each topic.
Why can a test with @EmbeddedKafka pass while production fails?

The embedded broker usually runs one node with replication factor 1, default configs, and maybe a different version, so it cannot reveal problems with min.insync.replicas, ACLs, TLS, topic configs created by a platform team, message size limits, or Schema Registry compatibility. Tests often also auto-create topics that production forbids. Run integration tests against a Testcontainers broker configured like production, and keep a smoke test in a real staging cluster.
Auto-commit vs commitSync vs commitAsync vs Spring's AckMode: which commit strategy?
subscribe() vs assign(): when do you skip the consumer group?
Null key vs record key vs custom partitioner?

| Null key | Record key | Custom partitioner
Partition chosen by | Sticky partitioner: fills a batch for one partition, then moves on | murmur2(key bytes) % number of partitions | Your code
Ordering | None across records | Per key | Whatever you design
Spread | Even over time | Skewed if a few keys are hot | You control it
Adding partitions | No effect | A key can move to a new partition; ordering breaks across the change | Depends
Typical use | Logs, metrics, clicks | Entity events: orderId, patientId | Rare: isolate a very large tenant
Rule of thumb: key by the entity whose events must stay in order. Use a custom partitioner only when a measured hot key forces it.
Avro vs Protobuf vs JSON Schema for Kafka messages?

| Avro | Protobuf | JSON Schema
Encoding | Compact binary without field names | Compact binary with field numbers | JSON text
Reader needs | The writer's schema (fetched from the registry by id) | Generated classes; field numbers carry meaning | Nothing to parse; schema used for validation
Safe change | Add a field with a default | Add a field with a new number | Add an optional property
Java tooling | avro-maven-plugin generates classes | protoc generates classes | Plain POJOs with Jackson
Readable on the topic | No | No | Yes
Interview tip: with the Confluent serializers each message starts with a magic byte and a 4-byte schema id, so a plain StringDeserializer shows garbage. Avro is the common choice in Kafka-centred platforms, Protobuf when teams already use gRPC, JSON Schema when readability matters more than size.
